What happens when 50 concurrent users attempt to book the exact same VIP shuttle seat at the exact same millisecond?
Double-booking? Frozen UI? Or a silent data race?
Most reservation systems look great in staging, but crumble under high-concurrency race conditions during peak flash sales.
In my latest architectural prototype, TransFlow AI — an executive intercity shuttle reservation platform for the Bandung – Jakarta corridor — I explored a resilient, production-grade architecture leveraging Feature-Sliced Design (FSD), Optimistic UI rollback mechanisms, and action-oriented AI via Model Context Protocol (MCP):
1️⃣ Optimistic UI with Instant Conflict Rollback:
Delivers instant 0ms perceived latency for passengers selecting seats. If a backend collision occurs (HTTP 409 Conflict), the UI immediately rolls back to its previous snapshot and gracefully marks the contested seat as held by another session—without breaking the user flow.
2️⃣ Anti-Race Distributed Atomic Lock:
Guarantees zero double-booking risk by securing seats through atomic locks with a 600-second (10-minute) TTL. Built-in stress test simulator executes 50 parallel bot threads competing for high-demand seats in real-time.
3️⃣ Action-Oriented AI via Model Context Protocol (MCP):
The AI Concierge isn’t just a passive conversational bot. Through MCP tools, it acts as an autonomous operational copilot:
• Queries real-time tollway sensors (`get_corridor_telemetry`) to monitor weather radar and traffic bottlenecks along the Cipularang expressway.
• Dynamically calculates estimated arrival times (`calculate_dynamic_eta`).
• Grounded RAG with real physical constraints: The Toyota HiAce Premio stands at 2.28m, strictly barring it from entering the elevated MBZ tollway (2.10m clearance gantry)—enforcing routing through the lower expressway for structural safety.
4️⃣ Authentic Top-Down Automotive Blueprint:
A precision cabin blueprint reflecting Indonesian automotive ergonomics: Right-Hand Drive (RHD) cockpit, curbside electric sliding door, and a distinct separation between 100% Flat Floor seats (Rows 1 & 2) vs. Rear Wheel Well arch protrusions (Row 3).
🛠️ Tech Stack: Next.js 15 (App Router), TypeScript, Feature-Sliced Design (FSD), Tailwind CSS, Model Context Protocol (MCP), Vector RAG, and jsPDF.

Over the past few months I've been building VenHub (Vendor Hub), an operations portal for vendors and internal teams at iForte Solusi Infotek. Field surveys and FTTH preventive maintenance used to run through many manual steps across several systems. VenHub moves that flow into one portal connected directly to Salesforce.

What VenHub does today: 
1. Connectivity Survey Salesforce sends surveys to vendors. Vendors fill in the Survey Form section by section, with photos per group. After submission, Salesforce creates or updates the Work Report and sends the status (Submitted, Approved or Rejected) back to VenHub.
2. Automatic PHS documents When a survey is Approved, the system calculates quantities against the PHS price list, generates the PDF, and uploads it to the Work Report in Salesforce. Failed deliveries retry automatically and can also be resent manually.
3. FTTH Preventive Maintenance Technicians submit a Customer ID, a category, and evidence photos. The photo count is validated against the category. Salesforce then sends the Work Order and Service Appointment status back.

What's next We plan to move more of the FTTH business process into VenHub, so vendors and internal teams work from one place.

Security and personal data protection VenHub holds customer and vendor data, so I built this in from the start, using Indonesia's Personal Data Protection Law (UU PDP) as the reference:
1. Email OTP login, plus mandatory Microsoft Authenticator for Super Admins and Admins
2. Temporary account lock after repeated failed logins, and automatic logout when idle
3. Personal data masked in logs and in views for roles that shouldn't see it
4. Access to personal data recorded: who, which role, which endpoint
5. Automatic data retention for logs, histories and notifications

Tech stack:
1. Backend: Go (Gin), PostgreSQL, JWT, TOTP
2. Frontend: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS v4, shadcn/ui, Zustand, React Hook Form + Zod, acting as a BFF so the browser never handles the API token
3. Integrations: Salesforce (Apex/LWC and REST), internal email service
4. Deployment: Docker & Jenkins

What I learned:
1. Two-way integration needs retries, idempotency, and clear logs, or small failures are hard to trace.
2. Security and privacy cost far less when built in from the beginning.
3. As developers, we have to solve problems, keep learning, and adapt to whatever comes up. We shouldn't idolize a single platform, because a developer needs to see the big picture and pick the tools that will actually help the company.

Thanks to the team who helped along the way Andrey Sholinka, Dwiky Kurniawan, Daffa Asyqar Ahmad Khalisheka, Karina Virgi, Viriya Putta, Jessica Jetje Joanna.

I just open-sourced "Servora" on GitHub under an MIT license. It is a self-hosted service, repair-and-maintenance platform built on .NET 10, SvelteKit, MySQL, and Hangfire.

Walk into almost any local repair shop or bengkel in Indonesia, and you will see the same setup: handwritten intake notes, scattered WhatsApp threads, and fragile spreadsheets. Enterprise CMMS platforms exist, sure, yet they are priced out of reach or far too rigid for a multi-branch AC technician team or a neighborhood phone shop.

Structuring Bankable Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) for Data Centers: Aligning Ramped MW Load Curves with Utility and IPP Financing

Securing reliable, clean electricity is the single largest operating determinant for data center platforms across Indonesia. Yet a structural mismatch frequently stalls financial close: utility and Independent Power Producer (IPP) financings require predictable, flat baseline revenues, whereas data center IT loads ramp gradually across multi-year tenant fit-outs. 

Whether contracting high-voltage grid supply, industrial-estate power, or clean energy firming across Batam, Jakarta, and West Java, misaligned power contracts create severe balance-sheet friction.

From an energy investment origination and enterprise risk governance perspective, data center PPAs reach institutional bankability only when ramped megawatt schedules, take-or-pay flexibility, and clean-energy attribution are structured upfront.

Signing rigid Day-1 full-capacity take-or-pay commitments without tenant lease alignment exposes developers to unrecoverable fixed charges before revenue ramps.

Six core pillars define bankable PPA structuring for data center origination across Indonesia:

 1. Phased Capacity Tranches & Ramped Load Curves: Bankable power agreements mirror realistic multi-year IT deployment schedules—stepping up contracted megawatts in defined tranches tied to substation energization and hall commissioning milestones.

 2. Calibrated Take-or-Pay & Minimum Offtake Bands: Balancing IPP debt-service certainty with data center utilization realities requires structured minimum-offtake bands, ramp-up grace periods, and clear capacity-reservation fees.

 3. Tenor Alignment Between Power Contracts and Anchor Leases: Institutional lenders scrutinize whether 15–20 year generation commitments align with hyperscale tenant lease tenors, renewal options, and pass-through tariff mechanics.

 4. Regulatory, Wheeling & Captive Supply Compliance: Power structures must adhere strictly to Indonesia’s electricity supply laws, industrial-estate business area (Wilayah Usaha) rules, and grid-connection frameworks to eliminate regulatory risk.

 5. 24/7 Clean Power Firming & Auditable REC Attribution: Global cloud and AI tenants increasingly require verifiable low-carbon power—integrating clean utility tariffs, solar-plus-BESS firming, and accredited Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) into contract schedules.

 6. Credit Support, Force Majeure Symmetry & ABAC Governance: Clear termination formulas, reciprocal delay remedies, creditworthy counterparty security, and strict anti-bribery and anti-corruption (ABAC) controls underpin institutional credit approval.

Water.

For Sunrise, liquidity isn't a trade-off. It's the cutoff: if a market can't be liquid, it doesn't launch.

That was Edward Zuo, Head of Operations at Sunrise, on our panel on building decentralized finance (DeFi) for Asia, with Wilbert Johan, Real-World Asset (RWA) Lead at Pendle, moderated by LevX, Lead Engineer at Giwater.

Wilbert said tokenized stocks face a basic question: why hold them on-chain instead of at a broker? Access is the first answer, for people who can't reach global markets or pass exchange checks. Ed agreed: someone in Japan or Indonesia often can't reach even local funds.

Pendle looks for redemption within 30 days and frequent payouts, Wilbert said, since DeFi users dislike quarterly distributions. Asian users have been moving into Treasury bill-backed stablecoins at fixed rates, and Pendle is building permissioned markets for verified users and institutions.

On new chains, Ed said a new asset has to reach the wallets, exchanges and aggregators where users are. Most Asian institutions are still waiting for regulatory clarity in Hong Kong, Japan and Korea.

Their one-line asks: connect institutional tokenized assets to DeFi (Wilbert), and let people trade in local currencies, not only US dollars (Ed).

A busy client may read your note before the CV, or instead of it. Make the note do the work.

Four lines I would put in every submission note:
1. Why this person, for this brief. Tie it to the client's must-haves. "5 years of Go, 2 of them on payments", not "strong backend engineer".
2. The gap, and what you checked. "No Kubernetes on the CV. Asked on the call: used it for a year in their last job." A shortlist that names its own gaps is easier to trust.
3. Notice period and start date. Ask for the clause in their contract. In Singapore the contract sets it, and MOM's defaults (1 day to 4 weeks, by length of service) apply only if the contract is silent. In Indonesia, someone resigning gives at least 30 days' written notice (PP 35/2021).
4. Salary expectation, and whether it fits the client's range.

🚀 Day 4/15 – First Complete Hibernate Program: Persisting Java Objects into MySQL | Java Backend Development Journey

Writing and executing an end-to-end database persistence workflow is where backend concepts truly come alive.

Today, I connected all the pieces from Day 3 and built my first complete Hibernate program to insert data into MySQL using modern Jakarta Persistence and Hibernate 6 standards.

📚 What I implemented and learned today:

✅ End-to-end application flow – Mapping a Java Student object through Hibernate (Session + Transaction + persist()) into MySQL (hibernate_db)
✅ Student Entity with Jakarta Persistence – Using @Entity, @Table, @Id, @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY), and @Column via jakarta.persistence
✅ XML mapping & configuration – Linking com.hibernate.entity.Student in hibernate.cfg.xml with hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto=update
✅ Reusable SessionFactory (HibernateUtil) – Encapsulating SessionFactory initialization in a dedicated utility class for clean resource reuse
✅ Transaction lifecycle in Main – Managing openSession(), beginTransaction(), session.persist(), tx.commit(), and session.close()
✅ SQL output & database verification – Inspecting Hibernate-generated INSERT queries in Eclipse and verifying persisted records directly in MySQL
✅ persist() vs. save() – Adopting JPA-standard persist() (void return, recommended) over legacy save() (deprecated in Hibernate 6)
✅ Troubleshooting setup issues – Resolving Unknown database, Access denied, and No suitable driver errors

💡 My biggest takeaway:

Understanding the lifecycle of SessionFactory, Session, and Transaction—along with why modern Hibernate 6 favors JPA-standard persist() over deprecated methods—builds clean, maintainable backend habits from day one.

Access to clean water continues to be an important infrastructure challenge across Southeast Asia, particularly as growing cities look for more sustainable alternatives to groundwater.

A good example comes from West Java, Indonesia, where PT WIKA Tirta Jaya Jatiluhur delivered the SPAM Regional Jatiluhur I water supply system, designed to provide reliable clean water access to more than380,000 residents across Jakarta, Bekasi, and Karawang.

The project involved an80-kilometre water supply system, with OpenFlows used to model hydraulic performance across the network, helping engineers evaluate pipeline sizing, balance pressure zones, and optimize pump station design.

The outcomes demonstrate the impact of bringing hydraulic modelling into a wider digital engineering workflow: up to 18% energy savings at pump stations, alongside faster project delivery and reduced design rework.

Beyond the numbers, this is a useful example of how hydraulic modelling can support the bigger picture of water infrastructure, balancing system performance, energy efficiency, sustainability, and long-term resilience.

For those involved in water supply projects, how early in the design process are hydraulic performance and energy efficiency being considered together?

Structuring Bankable Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) for Data Centers: Aligning Ramped MW Load Curves with Utility and IPP Financing

Securing reliable, clean electricity is the single largest operating determinant for data center platforms across Indonesia. Yet a structural mismatch frequently stalls financial close: utility and Independent Power Producer (IPP) financings require predictable, flat baseline revenues, whereas data center IT loads ramp gradually across multi-year tenant fit-outs. 

Whether contracting high-voltage grid supply, industrial-estate power, or clean energy firming across Batam, Jakarta, and West Java, misaligned power contracts create severe balance-sheet friction.

From an energy investment origination and enterprise risk governance perspective, data center PPAs reach institutional bankability only when ramped megawatt schedules, take-or-pay flexibility, and clean-energy attribution are structured upfront.

Signing rigid Day-1 full-capacity take-or-pay commitments without tenant lease alignment exposes developers to unrecoverable fixed charges before revenue ramps.

Six core pillars define bankable PPA structuring for data center origination across Indonesia:

 1. Phased Capacity Tranches & Ramped Load Curves: Bankable power agreements mirror realistic multi-year IT deployment schedules—stepping up contracted megawatts in defined tranches tied to substation energization and hall commissioning milestones.

 2. Calibrated Take-or-Pay & Minimum Offtake Bands: Balancing IPP debt-service certainty with data center utilization realities requires structured minimum-offtake bands, ramp-up grace periods, and clear capacity-reservation fees.

 3. Tenor Alignment Between Power Contracts and Anchor Leases: Institutional lenders scrutinize whether 15–20 year generation commitments align with hyperscale tenant lease tenors, renewal options, and pass-through tariff mechanics.

 4. Regulatory, Wheeling & Captive Supply Compliance: Power structures must adhere strictly to Indonesia’s electricity supply laws, industrial-estate business area (Wilayah Usaha) rules, and grid-connection frameworks to eliminate regulatory risk.

 5. 24/7 Clean Power Firming & Auditable REC Attribution: Global cloud and AI tenants increasingly require verifiable low-carbon power—integrating clean utility tariffs, solar-plus-BESS firming, and accredited Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) into contract schedules.

 6. Credit Support, Force Majeure Symmetry & ABAC Governance: Clear termination formulas, reciprocal delay remedies, creditworthy counterparty security, and strict anti-bribery and anti-corruption (ABAC) controls underpin institutional credit approval.
